# How Creative Earns Attention Across Screens


Neurons Co-Founder Mike Storm and Teads' Jonathan Lewis explain how creative shapes attention metrics in advertising, and why assets must adapt to every screen


By Cyrus Jabbari - Director, Global Content Strategy, Teads


November 18, 2026


> Attention is a leading indicator. It isn’t an outcome by itself. It’s an opener. Imagine I stop you at an event to give you my elevator pitch. I now have your attention, but if my pitch is bad, it’s gone and you won’t even remember it. That’s exactly the job an ad has every single time it gets in front of people.


Mike Storm captures the exact moment every ad is built for. Media and placement can earn a brand a second of someone’s time, but the creative decides what happens next. That’s why creative belongs in every conversation about attention metrics in advertising, and why the brands seeing the strongest business outcomes plan creative quality and media placement together.


As part of ou *r Cut Through the Noise* series, Mike and Jonathan Lewis, Global Head of Teads Studio, share their perspectives on how much creative contributes to attention, which elements earn it and carry it through to the brand, why each asset should be adapted to the screen it appears on, and why pre-testing belongs in every campaign workflow.


Teads Studio works closely with Neurons, using its predictive AI to analyze creative assets for visual attention, emotional response, and cognitive appeal before assets go live. Our *L’Atelier* co-creation workshops then put those insights to work alongside brands and their creative agencies.


For Swiss window manufacturer 4B and its media agency Konnex, a few targeted edits to existing videos made all the difference. Adding distinct start and end cards with the logo, alongside captions for sound-off viewing, helped the optimized versions deliver a[64% lift in brand awareness and a 29% lift in ad recall](https://www.neuronsinc.com/cases/teads-media-platform) compared with the originals.


## **Why Creative Quality Shapes Attention Metrics in Advertising**


Creative quality has long been recognized as the main driver of effectiveness. Research by Analytic Partners, drawing on studies of 750 brands across 45 countries, found that[two-thirds (66%) of video advertising success comes from how compelling the creative is](https://www.teads.com/blog/creative-catalyst-for-ad-effectiveness/2716/) , outweighing targeting, placement, and timing. Teads’ own testing points the same way: across 23,072 creative assets measured with Kantar in 2023, Teads Studio-optimized versions achieved statistically significant lifts in ad recall compared with the original assets.

Even so, Mike observes a hyperfocus on media and audiences when brands read attention metrics in advertising, largely because they’re the easiest levers to measure. Neurons’ research reveals differences of **up to 500%** in the attention two ads can earn in the same environment. A weak creative might hold a viewer for less than a second, whereas a strong one in the same placement can hold them for five seconds or more, giving the brand far more opportunity to build a memory that[drives measurable campaign outcomes](https://www.teads.com/lp/performance-advertising/) ..


Jonathan Lewis, Global VP of Studio at Teads, frames this through the attention ceiling concept developed by Karen Nelson Field. Every placement has a ceiling on the attention it can earn. A sound-on, full-screen video ad has more elasticity than a small banner fixed to the bottom of a page, so he sees placement and creative as two sides of the same coin:


- **Placement Sets the Ceiling:** The format and environment define how much attention an ad can realistically earn.
- **Creative Determines the Result:** The quality of the asset decides how close the ad gets to that ceiling, and how much of the attention it earns turns into brand impact.


## **The Creative Elements Behind Attention and Brand Outcomes**


While effective creative vary by brand, vertical, and context, Mike and Jonathan highlight five consistent signals that capture consumer attention and link it through to the brand:


1. **A Clear Focal Point:** Uncluttered creative gives the eye one place to land.
2. **Human Faces:** People engage instantly with other people, making faces one of the strongest drivers of consumer attention.
3. **Emotional Intensity:** Research consistently shows that ads generating an emotional response are better remembered and tend to perform better.
4. **Distinctive Brand Assets:** Sonic cues, characters, and a recognizable color palette let viewers identify the brand without needing to see the logo.
5. **Product Features:** For[performance and lower-funnel objectives](https://www.teads.com/lp/performance-advertising/) , clear product messaging carries more weight, balanced with brand assets to support both sales and long-term growth.


Mike stresses the importance of balance: a celebrity or influencer can hold attention so completely that viewers remember the face while forgetting the brand. Neurons recommends capturing attention with faces in the first two seconds while placing the brand or product in that same moment.


**Attention opens the door, and the creative has to use it: an ad can earn strong attention and still create annoyance or build ad memory without building brand memory.**


For that reason, Neurons reads attention metrics in advertising alongside emotional engagement, trust, and avoidance, giving brands a fuller view of how an ad is likely to land before money is spent.


### **Four Common Creative Pitfalls That Erode Attention**


- **Late Branding:** Attention peaks in the first couple of seconds on digital, so a late brand reveal is often missed.
- **A Slow Start:** Mike has seen a black screen in the first 500 milliseconds drive a sharp rise in drop-off, particularly in scrolling environments where viewers move on instantly.
- **Cognitive Overload:** Too many competing logos, words, and colors make the message harder to process.
- **Platform Mismatch:** Opening a video with dialogue on a sound-off platform is an immediate miss with viewers.


## **Adapting Creative to Every Screen**


Context shapes creative performance on two levels. The first is **format adaptation** , where Neurons regularly sees ads that aren’t optimized for their placement perform at less than half the level of optimized ads on attention, emotion, and memory.


The second is **topical context** . A travel ad running alongside an article about someone traveling through Thailand reaches a reader whose brain is already tuned in to vacations, so the ad lands as relevant from the first second. This is where premium publisher environments give creative an advantage across an[omnichannel advertising strategy](https://www.teads.com/omnichannel/) .


Jonathan’s advice is to build once and build for flexibility. The same asset can perform very differently from one platform to another, and a TV commercial shipped unchanged across every screen leaves attention on the table. Creative that keeps its core idea while adapting to each placement benefits twice, reaching closer to each placement’s attention ceiling while campaign creative consistency compounds across screens.


> Build once, but build with enough flexibility that it can adapt to different placements and platforms, while still retaining creative consistency, because there’s a positive compounding effect when you can retain that consistency across platforms.


[Connected TV (CTV) advertising](https://www.teads.com/lp/connected-tv-advertising/) brings new canvases that reward purpose-built design. Jonathan points to the Smart TV home screen as one of them, a placement many advertisers don’t yet have assets built for. Creative designed for the space pays off, and our eye-tracking study with the MediaMento Institute found that[3D creative on CTV HomeScreen captured attention 29% faster](https://www.teads.com/blog/new-study-teads-ctv-homescreen-drives-superior-attention-and-brand-impact-across-premium-video-advertising/7660/) and held it longer than standard formats.


Furthermore, CTV also strengthens attention measurement. Mike notes that CTV now gives brands TV measurement data at a scale not seen since the early days of panel-based ratings, which makes it possible to connect predicted attention to outcomes on the biggest screen in the home.


## **Attention Optimization Starts Before Launch**


The most important shift for creative mirrors what attention metrics in advertising have already changed in media buying: moving attention optimization out of post-campaign reports and into pre-launch workflows.


Both Mike and Jonathan see too much creative testing still happening after the fact, when measuring attention in advertising can now start at the concept stage. Predictive AI makes it practical to test every asset in advance, and Mike believes pre-testing should be a fundamental part of every workflow.


Jonathan is clear that predictive scores are a leading indicator rather than a guarantee of performance, especially lower in the funnel where pricing and timing play a larger role. Used across the campaign lifecycle, they connect attention and campaign performance for creative and media teams alike:


- **Pre-Launch Testing:** Assets are scored and optimized before production is locked.[Teads Predictive AI](https://www.teads.com/blog/teads-predictive-ai-shaping-the-future-of-creative-effectiveness/9284/) , built on eye-tracking and neuroscience data, scores focus, cognitive demand, engagement, memory, and impact.
- **In-Flight Optimization:** Attention metrics in advertising show which formats and creatives are performing in market, so delivery can shift toward them while the campaign is live.
- **Post-Campaign Learning:** Brand lift results validate the predictions and feed the next round of testing.


> Brands should pre-test pretty much every single ad that goes to market. They may not need to fix every one, but having a score means you go to market with an educated decision. You know this ad will be great at product attention but weaker at brand attention, and at least you know you’re not going to market blindly.


## **Looking Ahead: Breaking Down Creative and Media Silos**


Mike believes the brands that win in an attention-driven market will be the ones that stop working in silos. When insights, brand, and media teams each work from a different data set, optimization stalls. Connecting creative data such as predicted attention and emotion scores with media, audience, brand, and outcome data gives every team the same view of what’s working.


As attention metrics in advertising become part of how campaigns are planned, the advantage will sit with brands that treat creative as a measurable driver of performance, test it before launch, and adapt it to every screen it runs on.


> The brands that will win are the ones that bring their data and learnings together, and don’t silo the different parts of the campaign journey. That means connecting creative data, like predicted attention and emotion scores, to media, outcome, audience, and brand data, and using it as one combined data set.
